title: 3 Simple Ways To Check For Understanding
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies checking for understanding as a common weak spot among the teachers he observes, warning that sending students to independent work without confirming they understand leads to a flood of raised hands, reteaching, boredom, and learned helplessness. He rejects the vague, commonly used question 'Are there any questions?' and instead offers three low-tech, fast techniques: individual whiteboards that students hold up on signal to show their answers; a thumbs up/thumbs down response to a direct yes-or-no question; and 'negative questions,' where the teacher asks who does NOT understand rather than who does, which shifts responsibility onto students to speak up. He describes each technique's mechanics in practical detail, including sample phrasing teachers can use. The piece concludes that these techniques enable a classroom to run smoothly with real independence, faster growth, and access to a productive flow state.
points: Failing to check for understanding before independent work is identified as a common weakness that leads to reteaching, boredom, and learned helplessness.
The vague question 'Are there any questions?' is explicitly rejected as insufficient.
Three concrete techniques are offered: individual whiteboards, thumbs up/thumbs down responses, and 'negative questions' asking who does not understand.
'Negative questions' work by shifting the burden of speaking up onto students rather than the teacher guessing who is confused.
Effective checks for understanding are framed as enabling faster academic growth and a productive 'flow state' during independent work.
quotes: In observing teachers, one common area of weakness is checking for understanding. Not every teacher, of course. But many.
Often, the most I hear from teachers is “Are there any questions?” Which just doesn’t cut it.
Whiteboards give you all the information you need to decide whether to begin independent work right away or continue teaching.
The way it works is that you’ll ask them not if they understand, but if they don’t understand.
This puts the onus on them, makes them responsible to speak up, and leaves them with no excuse not to do the work.
They bring silence, instill true independence, and trigger the highly pleasurable flow state, where students get lost in their work.
